content: Fragmented sleep patterns are characterized by individuals sleeping at various times throughout the day and for shorter durations during the night. For instance, in many Mediterranean and Latin American cultures, people take a siesta, which involves sleeping for a period in the afternoon. In nomadic or hunter-gatherer societies, sleep often occurs intermittently throughout the day or night, depending on situational demands. Horses and other herbivorous ungulates are capable of sleeping while standing but must lie down for REM sleep, as this stage induces muscular atony. Giraffes, for example, only need to lie down for REM sleep for a few minutes at a time. Bats, on the other hand, sleep while hanging upside down. Certain aquatic mammals and some bird species exhibit unihemispheric slow-wave sleep, where one hemisphere of the brain remains awake while the other sleeps. Birds and mammals experience cycles of non-REM and REM sleep similar to humans, although birds’ sleep cycles are significantly shorter, and they do not lose muscle tone to the same extent as most mammals. While many animals sleep, defining neurological sleep states in lower-order animals is challenging. In these species, sleep is identified through behavioral characteristics such as minimal movement, species-specific postures, and reduced responsiveness to external stimuli. Sleep in these animals is quickly reversible, unlike hibernation or coma, and sleep deprivation is followed by longer or deeper sleep. Many mammalian species sleep for a substantial portion of each 24-hour period during early life stages. However, killer whales and some dolphins do not sleep during the first month after birth. Regarding the longest periods without sleep, several individuals have claimed records depending on how sleep is defined. Thai Ngoc, born in 1942, claimed in 2006 to have been awake for 33 years (11,700 nights) following a fever in 1973, though other reports suggest he stopped sleeping in 1976 without a known trigger. Despite his claims, Ngoc reportedly suffered no significant health effects other than a minor decline in liver function. However, some reports indicate he later experienced health issues due to his lack of sleep. In January 2005, RIA Novosti reported on Fyodor Nesterchuk from Ukraine, who claimed to have not slept for over 20 years. Local physician Fyodor Koshel examined him extensively but could not induce sleep. Nesterchuk reportedly did not exhibit the usual adverse effects of sleep deprivation. Some researchers suggest that individuals like Nesterchuk may experience microsleep episodes, brief moments of sleep lasting seconds or fractions of a second, which are often not remembered. This phenomenon could explain the perceived lack of sleep in such cases. Randy Gardner holds the Guinness World Record for the longest intentional period without sleep. In 1965, at the age of 18, Gardner stayed awake for 264 hours (approximately 11 days) as part of a high school science project. During this time, he experienced significant impairments in concentration, motivation, perception, and other higher mental functions. However, he recovered normal cognitive abilities after a few nights of sleep. On May 25, 2007, the BBC reported that Tony Wright surpassed Gardner’s record by staying awake for 11 days and nights. However, the Guinness Book of Records no longer supports sleep deprivation records due to associated health risks. A rare case involves Rhett Lamb, a three-year-old boy from St. Petersburg, Florida, who has only slept for one to two hours per day over the past three years. He has a rare condition known as Arnold-Chiari malformation, where brain tissue protrudes into the spinal canal, and the skull exerts pressure on the affected brain region. It remains unclear whether this malformation directly contributes to his sleep deprivation. Rhett underwent experimental surgery to address the issue.
